results.title: Can you resell GPU compute you already bought?
highlights:
## Reserved, on-demand, and spot are three different products

A GPU price isn’t one number. It depends on what you’re buying.

- On-demand is pay-by-the-second, no commitment. Modal’s public pricing page, checked August 2026, lists on-demand serverless rates of $7.10/hr for B300 and $3.95/hr for H100 SXM5. Lambda’s public pricing page, also checked August 2026, lists on-demand H100 SXM at $3.99 to $4.29/hr depending on cluster size.
- Reserved is a forward commitment, usually one to three years, cheaper per hour because you committed. Compute Exchange’s public reserved-GPU pricing page, published April 10, 2026, states that a one-year reserved H100 SXM contract runs near $1.89/hr and a three-year reserved H100 PCIe contract near $1.84/hr, against an on-demand H100 SXM rate of about $2.99/hr quoted on the same page.
- Spot is unreserved, interruptible capacity priced off whatever happens to be idle. It can be cheaper than both, or briefly more expensive, depending on demand that minute.

A reservation is a forward contract. You agree today to a price and a quantity of compute delivered later, and you get a discount off on-demand for it.

Put $1.89/hr reserved (Compute Exchange, April 10, 2026) next to $3.95/hr on-demand (Modal, August 2026) and the reservation looks like an easy win, roughly 2.1 times cheaper. But a forward contract only pays off if you actually use what you locked in, or can sell it to someone who will.

...

The market already has an answer to “what if I overcommitted.” Here’s one public example, based only on what the company says about itself.

Compute Exchange runs a public marketplace for reserved and secondary GPU hardware. Its blog post on reserved GPU marketplaces, published March 4, 2026, describes more secondary-market activity as expiring A100 and H100 contracts come back on the market. It puts refurbished 2-year-old H100 units at roughly 30 to 40 percent of their historical peak price.

The same post says this resale activity had not, as of its March 2026 publish date, brought prices down the way a buyer might hope. It describes H100 pricing as having risen a further 15 to 20 percent over the period it covers, with several neocloud providers announcing more increases.

...

This isn’t hypothetical. It already happened with GPUs. Introl’s analysis of the H100 rental market, published January 12, 2026, describes H100 prices falling from an earlier peak of about $8 per hour to a more recent range of $2.85 to $3.50 per hour, a decline it puts at roughly 64 percent. Introl dates that peak to late 2024.

results.title: $0.10 versus $0.47 per million tokens: that is the real cost gap between two GPUs running the same model. The GPU with the higher hourly rate turns out to be the cheaper … | Spheron Network
highlights:
$0.10 versus $0.47 per million tokens: that is the real cost gap between two GPUs running the same model. The GPU with the higher hourly rate turns out to be the cheaper one per token.

H200 costs $4.96 an hour on demand. B200 costs $7.50, about 50% more. On the sticker, H200 looks cheaper.

But hourly rate is not cost per token. B200 running FP4 processes far more tokens in that hour. Divide cost by tokens processed and the ranking flips. B200 lands at $0.10 per million tokens, H200 at $0.47, a 4.7x gap. We calculated both figures from the source's throughput and pricing data, so check them against your own model.

FP4 is a lower-precision format that lets a GPU do more math per second, at some accuracy cost. That cost is small for most language tasks but larger for math-heavy or vision workloads, so test your model first. B200's native FP4 support is what drives that gap.

- Pick B200 if your workload tolerates FP4 and you want tokens per dollar at scale.
- Pick H200 if you need FP8 or FP16 precision, or B200 capacity is not available.

results.title: Oblivus Blog | More Capacity in the Oblivus GPU Marketplace
highlights:
# More Capacity, More Choice: The Oblivus GPU Marketplace Just Got Bigger

26 August 2026

## The best GPU for your workload should always be one click away.

When we launched the Oblivus GPU Marketplace, the goal was simple: make it easy to find GPU compute and easy for hardware owners to put idle machines to work. Since then, the single most common request we have heard from builders has also been simple— more. More GPUs available right now. More models to choose from. More places to run.

Today, that request is answered. We have connected additional GPU supply into the marketplace, and it is live in your console now. The catalogue you browse is significantly deeper than it was last month, and it keeps refreshing as capacity comes and goes.

## What actually changed

Nothing about how you rent has changed. What changed is how much there is to rent.

- A deeper catalogue: many more live listings to browse, from single-GPU boxes for prototyping and inference to multi-GPU nodes for serious training runs.
- More GPU models: a wider spread of hardware generations, so you can match the card to the job instead of taking whatever happens to be free.
- More locations: a broader geographic footprint, which matters when you care about latency, data residency, or simply want a second option when one region is busy.
- More price points: a real spread between budget capacity and top-tier accelerators, so you can trade cost against speed deliberately.

In short: the marketplace stopped being a shortlist and started being a proper market.

## Same flow. Just more to choose from.

Every listing still shows you what you need to make a decision before you spend a cent: GPU model and count, VRAM, CPU, RAM, storage, location, hourly price, reliability score, CUDA version, maximum rental duration, and verification status.

And the workflow is unchanged:

- Filter and sort by price, reliability, or verified listings to narrow a long list down fast.
- Rent in a click—set your machine password and launch.
- Pay by the second at the listed hourly rate. No minimums, no rounding up to the hour.
- Work from the console using the built-in marketplace terminal, and stop your rental whenever you are done.
